title: What the commemoration of the 235th anniversary of Bois Caïman means for Haiti’s memory and future
content:
Enslaved people united to resist colonial rule

Originally published on Global Voices

Participants in the Bois Caïman commemoration at Hotel Roi Christophe (Cap-Haïtien). Photo courtesy Kenbe Kapow, used with permission.

The night of August 14, 1791, marked the beginning of a series of events that changed the world. A large group of enslaved people and rebel leaders met at Bwa Kayiman (Bois Caïman), a historic site located in Haiti’s Northern Department, in the town of Plaine-du-Nord.

Under the leadership of the houngan (Vodou priest) Dutty Boukman and manbo (priestess) Cécile Fatiman — along with key resistance leaders — the gathering brought together enslaved people from different plantations for a clandestine religious and political ceremony. They invoked the lwa and ancestral spiritual forces, seeking their protection and strength for the struggle ahead.
snippet:
Enslaved people united to resist colonial rule

title: As Casablanca’s music scene grows, its musicians struggle
content:
A cultural boom built on unstable, undocumented work

Originally published on Global Voices

Band performing live at Le Backstage. Photo by Le Backstage, used with permission.

It’s 7:00 p.m. on a Tuesday night. Beer mugs clatter and conversations fill the timeworn hall of an old brasserie in downtown Casablanca, Morocco. Walid Rakik, a 28-year-old musician, sits in the back booth, speaking to the house pianist. Rakik is the headliner, accompanied by a young darbouka player. For Rakik, this means a three-way split of tonight’s tips, the only form of payment they will receive.

At 11:00 p.m., Rakik finishes his first set and makes the quick dash to a Spanish-themed late-night spot for his second set.

Rakik’s daily reality, like that of many musicians in Casablanca, remains barely visible behind the polished façades of the city’s nightspots. A labor force of ambience, part artisan, part gig-worker, operates at the periphery of the city’s cultural landscape. 

For Rakik, however, live music is not his only occupation. Like many musicians in Casablanca, he fits performances around other work, treating nightlife gigs as a secondary source of income and a way to remain active professionally.
snippet:
A cultural boom built on unstable, undocumented work

title: The people behind the numbers: Bringing the reality of Turkish prisons to light
content:
A statistic alone does not change society

Originally published on Global Voices

Silivri Prison in Turkey. Image from Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 4.0.

This article was produced by Ahmet Kavruk from the group Gündem Hapishane in Türkiye through the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project. It was implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In late 2025, prisons in Türkiye became more visible than they had been in a long time. The 11th Judicial Package, a legislative reform that became law in December, was debated for days on television, in newspapers, and on social media. Sentencing regulations, claims of early release, and changes to the penal system were at the forefront of public discourse. However, as the debates intensified, another issue came to light: Many people discussing the same topic did not actually have the same information.
snippet:
A statistic alone does not change society

title: ‘Pay-by-the-day’ living in Pereira: The forgotten survivors of Colombia’s earthquake
content:
They may have survived the earthquake, but many were left without shelter, support, or recognition

Originally published on Global Voices

Without an official figure, volunteers estimate that nearly 400 people affected by the earthquake are sheltering in La Libertad Park. Photos by Jeimi Villamizar. Colombia, 2026. Used with permission.

A crack divides the residencia on 14th Street in Pereira in two. Bricks from the boarding house’s façade and pieces of its collapsed roof lie on the ground. Windows without glass and yellow caution tape across the front warn of the risk of collapse.

From the outside, it is hard to understand why it is still standing — perhaps much like the way it remained standing for the past decade, thanks to people looking for a roof over their heads for less than COP 17,000 (USD 5) a day. Before the earth moved and turned it into a memory, one of the rooms on its three floors was home to Laura*, her two daughters* [*these three names have been changed to protect their privacy] and her husband.
snippet:
They may have survived the earthquake, but many were left without shelter, support, or recognition

title: Can a new national peace policy fix Nigeria’s security problems?
content:
Nigeria's National Peace Policy is a framework intended to bring greater coordination to conflict prevention and peacebuilding

Originally published on Global Voices

ACC. H. O. Idoko, Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps (NSCDC) representative, speaking at the National Peace Policy review in Abuja, 4-6 August, 2026. Photo by Triple Peace Africa. Used with permission.

The world is spending more on war and defense than ever before. Global military expenditure reached a record USD 2.7 trillion in 2024, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), as governments increased spending amid wars in Europe and Western Asia and growing security tensions elsewhere. 

Africa is part of that trend. Military expenditure on the continent rose by 8.5 percent in 2025 to USD 58.2 billion. Nigeria’s spending rose even more sharply, increasing by 55 percent to USD 2.1 billion, according to SIPRI.
snippet:
Nigeria's National Peace Policy is a framework intended to bring greater coordination to conflict prevention and peacebuilding

title: Reforms on Malaysia’s ‘draconian’ Peaceful Assembly Act encounter further delays
content:
Civil society groups are demanding a timeline for when the government will reform the restrictive legislation

Originally published on Global Voices

Marchers during the Bersih (change) protest in Kuala Lumpur in 2011. Photo by Hafiz Noor Shams, uploaded on Wikipedia, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported

This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Human rights advocates are calling on the Malaysian government to amend the Peaceful Assembly Act, which contains several provisions that police and local authorities use to undermine, disrupt, and even criminalize protests and public assemblies. Despite months of promises to amend the controversial provision, the government has continually delayed reforms.

The law passed in 2012 and has been weaponized by successive governments to file harassment charges against protest organizers and leaders of civil society groups.

title: North Macedonia’s independence should not be commemorated by glorifying war criminals
content:
Death does not erase the verdict — or the responsibility of officials who turn a convicted war criminal into a hero

Originally published on Global Voices

Bardhyl Jashari, executive director of Metamorphosis Foundation. Photo in a private archive, used with permission.

This article by Bardhyl Jashari was first published in Albanian on portalb.mk on August 31, 2026. An edited version is republished here under a content-sharing agreement between Global Voices and the Metamorphosis Foundation.

Death does not erase the verdict. When a war criminal is placed on a pedestal by government officials, it undermines the dignity of the victims, weakens the rule of law, harms the very idea of North Macedonia as a multiethnic society, and compromises the country’s European vision. In the year when North Macedonia marks 35 years of independence, we should have understood by now that a state is not built by glorifying war criminals.
snippet:
Death does not erase the verdict — or the responsibility of officials who turn a convicted war criminal into a hero

title: What does folklore have to say? It helps uncover untold facets of Indigenous stories overlooked for generations
content:
Some interesting stories I came across during documentation of Tharu Indigenous folklore

Originally published on Global Voices

A Tharu woman from Kailali District of Western Nepal with tattoos on her legs. Photo by Indu Tharu, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.

As a child, I used to sit with my grandmother near a borais (a small earthen pot used to make fire) during the harsh winter days. I would listen to her stories of benevolent and malevolent characters — djinns, spirits, ghosts, witches and wizards, trees, birds and animals that had special significance in the Tharu culture and tradition. She used to sing folk songs and then explain their meaning.

title: The people who live in cities must have a say in how they are shaped: Notes from the Common City Conference
content:
The right to adequate housing is recognized under international law

Originally published on Global Voices

Kehinde Adegboyega, co-founder and executive director of Human Rights Journalists Network at Housing Rights conference. Photo used with permission.

Across African cities, urban growth often comes at a cost that hits the poorest residents hardest: Forced evictions, informal settlements razed for redevelopment projects, and land decisions made with little or no consultation with the people who live there. In Lagos, Cape Town, and beyond, these patterns raise a question that goes beyond urban planning: Who gets to decide the future of a city, and whose knowledge counts in that decision?

That question came up at the Common City Conference in Uppsala, Sweden, where scholars, activists, and grassroots organizers gathered to discuss housing, urban justice, and the right to the city. Among them was Kehinde Adegboyega, co-founder and executive director of the Human Rights Journalists Network Nigeria (HRJN), invited to present a panel on “Resisting Authoritarian Urbanism in Sub-Saharan Africa: Counter-Knowledge and the Housing Commons in Lagos and Cape Town.”
snippet:
The right to adequate housing is recognized under international law

title: In turbulent times, football brings Haiti hope
content:
Many sports parks are located in areas controlled by gangs, but Haitian football is not dead

Originally published on Global Voices

Feature image of a football in the colours of the Haitian flag, on a football field, created using Canva Pro elements.

In Haiti, the sport of football creates social cohesion: despite their differences, people from all classes come together on the field. Children from wealthy families, poor backgrounds, and middle-class homes alike get the opportunity to mix by either playing for the same football team, or facing one another as opponents.

The same approach informs how players are chosen for the national team; all social categories are represented based solely on the quality of each player’s talent. Spectators have a similar experience, in that people from all walks of life cross paths to celebrate, support their teams, and share moments of victory or defeat.
snippet:
Many sports parks are located in areas controlled by gangs, but Haitian football is not dead

title: Maternity leave is expanding in Bangladesh, but garment workers still struggle for childcare
content:
“The breastfeeding room was always there. But there was no-one to bring my baby to me.”

Originally published on Global Voices

Workers at a garment factory in Gazipur, Bangladesh. Image via Flickr by Solidarity Center. CC BY 2.0.

In April 2026, Bangladesh’s Parliament amended the country’s labour law, extending maternity benefits for eligible workers from 112 to 120 days, or approximately four months. Yet for many women in the country’s garment factories, the harder question begins when that leave ends: Who cares for their babies while they return to shifts that may last 10 to 14 hours?

The pressure is not limited to garment workers. Across Bangladesh, working mothers often depend on relatives or informal care networks, while affordable, quality childcare remains limited. The International Labour Organization (ILO) has noted that Bangladesh’s traditional family-dependent care system is under pressure as patterns of work and migration change. For low-income workers with long or unpredictable hours, that gap can be especially difficult.
snippet:
“The breastfeeding room was always there. But there was no-one to bring my baby to me.”
